entry.title: One Knob, 19x Latency: What I Learned Benchmarking vLLM on a Single GPU
entry.summary:
I built a small serving harness that measures latency, throughput, AND output drift per config. It found a 19x latency cliff on a single knob, a 3.6x model speed gap — and a reasoning model that can't reproduce its own outputs at temperature 0.
Scope note, first paragraph as promised: one RTX 3060, two models (Swallow-8B AWQ, llm-jp-1.8B bf16), short prompts, synthetic Poisson arrivals — not production traces. No human judged anything; drift is exact output-hash match. First surprise: max-num-seqs 32 vs 128 showed identical numbers across fixed-concurrency and Poisson loads. The server never broke a sweat, so the knob looked irrelevant. It isn't — my load was just too polite. I added a stress arm (64 concurrent, 256 output tokens) and the same comparison became TTFT p50 8.3s vs 0.43s. Same models, same prompts, one knob: 19x. TPOT stayed flat throughout (16→28ms) — textbook prefill queueing. Lesson I'll reuse everywhere: config comparisons REQUIRE a stress arm; gentle benchmarks can't tell servers apart. Same stress, different model: llm-jp-1.8B serves at 119ms TTFT vs Swallow-8B's 432ms, 28.5 vs 15.1 req/s. Unsurprising direction, useful magnitude — and a deployment footnote: llm-jp runs under vLLM's own kernels while stock transformers trips on its RoPE config. Know your stack's two paths. The quality probe — 50 frozen prompts hashed per config, there to catch quality regressions — caught something else: the same Swallow server, identical requests, 10/50 outputs differ run to run (12/50 across restarts). A non-reasoning model on the same harness: identical ×3. Think-mode sampling leaks through temperature 0. If your production system assumes deterministic serving (caching, evals, replay), verify it per model — don't assume it. Asyncio+aiohttp client, fixed + Poisson loads, TTFT/TPOT p50/p95, error rates, per-run JSONL, frozen quality set. Client-only venv; the server lives in sibling venvs. 3 tests against a fake SSE server run in CI (no GPU needed). All numbers, prompts, and hashes are linked below.

entry.title: Rebuild or Repair: How to Decide What Your Business Website Actually Needs
entry.summary: Every old website reaches the same argument: the owner wants to tear it down and start fresh, the developer suggests fixes, and both are guessing. Here is a calmer way to decide, based on what actually drives results. If the site loads fast, works on phones, and the content is mostly right, you probably need a refresh, not a rebuild. New design on the key pages, clearer calls to action, updated photos, fixed forms. This costs a fraction of a rebuild and you keep all your search rankings, which a rebuild can easily damage. Some sites cannot be saved by paint. Rebuild when the site was built on dead technology, when every small change breaks something else, when it is not mobile friendly at its core, or when the business itself has changed so much that the old structure fights the new message. These are structural problems. Cosmetics will not fix them. One, does the site bring enquiries today, even a few. A site that converts a little is worth improving. A site that converts nothing may be cheaper to replace. Two, can a developer make changes without fear. If simple edits take days and break things, the foundation is the problem. Three, does the design match what you sell now. If the business outgrew the message, no amount of polishing the old words will do. If you rebuild, protect your search presence: keep the same page addresses where you can, redirect the ones you change, and launch with the content that already ranks. Most rebuild disasters are not design failures. They are traffic failures. A website is a tool, not a monument. Fix the tool when you can, replace it when you must, and never let either choice be driven by boredom. This is how we advise clients at Cloudlift Tech: honest audits first, rebuilds only when the numbers say so. You can see our web work and the thinking behind it at cloudlifttech.com. The right answer is the boring one: whatever costs less and converts more.

entry.title: How to delete EVERY copy of a duplicate line (not just the extras)
entry.summary:
Most dedupe tools keep one copy of each repeated line and delete the rest. But sometimes that's the wrong result. Sometimes a value that appears twice is bad data, and you want it gone completely — only the lines that appear exactly once should survive. Real examples: sign-ups who registered twice and must be excluded entirely, customers who appear in two monthly exports when you only want the new ones, or SKUs that show up twice in a supplier file with different prices (keep neither until a human checks). Here are the ways to do it, from spreadsheets to one paste. =UNIQUE(A2:A1000, FALSE, TRUE)
The third argument is the trick: TRUE means "only rows that occur exactly once". Every copy of a repeated value is excluded. Put this next to your data and fill down: =COUNTIF($A:$A, A2)

entry.title: Cloud Bill Creep: The Small Mistakes That Quietly Drain a Business Budget
entry.summary: Cloud bills rarely explode. They creep. Ten dollars here for a forgotten test server, forty there for storage nobody looks at, and by year end the business is paying for a ghost town of resources. Here are the leaks I see most often, and the simple fixes. Development and test machines run all night and all weekend for nobody. Schedule them to shut down outside work hours. For many teams this one change cuts the compute bill nearly in half, with zero effect on anyone's workday. Old backups, duplicate uploads, logs kept forever. Storage is cheap per unit and expensive in aggregate. Put a simple rule in place: everything gets a review date, and anything past it gets archived or deleted. Assign one person to own the monthly cleanup. Most cloud servers are bought bigger than needed, just in case. Monitor actual usage for a month, then right size. Downgrading a server takes minutes and the savings repeat every month. If a workload runs all the time, reserved pricing beats pay as you go by a wide margin. Businesses leave this money on the table because nobody did the one hour of math. Do the math. Set billing alerts at levels that mean something, and send them to a person, not a dead inbox. A quiet alert is the same as no alert. Cloud cost control is not a once a year project. It is a monthly habit: fifteen minutes with the bill and a short list. We run this discipline for our own infrastructure and for clients at Cloudlift Tech, where right sized cloud setups are part of every project we ship. Our approach to lean, honest cloud work is at cloudlifttech.com. The cloud is not expensive. Unwatched cloud is.

entry.title: Layer 2 Scaling Solutions
entry.summary: Layer 2 scaling solutions help blockchains like Ethereum process more activity without forcing every transaction to happen directly on the base chain. Ethereum’s main network is secure and decentralized, but blockspace is limited. When demand rises, fees increase and users can get priced out. Layer 2s address this by moving transaction activity to scaling systems that sit around Ethereum while still using it for settlement, security, data posting, or verification. The most important Layer 2 designs today are rollups. Rollups process transactions off-chain, bundle them together, and post data or proofs back to Ethereum. This makes transactions cheaper and faster while keeping a connection to Ethereum’s trust foundation.
